subject: environmental-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Species richness is best defined as:
options: The genetic variation within a species
The variety of habitats in a region
The relative abundance of each species
The total number of different species present
questions.explain: Species richness is simply a count of how many different species are present, irrespective of their abundance.

questions.q: Which fishing practice is most associated with high levels of bycatch and seabed damage?
questions.explain: Bottom trawling drags nets across the seabed, causing high bycatch and physical habitat destruction.

questions.q: Two communities both contain 5 species. Community A has one dominant species and four rare ones; Community B has five equally abundant species. Community B has higher:
questions.explain: Evenness reflects how equally individuals are distributed among species, so equal abundances give higher evenness.

questions.q: r-strategist species are typically characterised by:
options: Many offspring, rapid reproduction, small body size and little parental care
Stable populations close to carrying capacity
Few offspring with high parental care and long lifespans
questions.explain: r-strategists produce many small offspring quickly with little parental care, enabling rapid colonisation of unstable environments.

questions.q: The Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) of a fishery is the:
options: Total biomass of fish in the sea
Catch that maximises short-term profit only
Largest catch that can be taken indefinitely without depleting the stock
Minimum catch needed to feed a population
questions.explain: MSY is the largest catch that can be removed year after year while keeping the stock stable long-term.

questions.q: A pyramid of energy is always upright (broad base, narrow top) because:
options: Producers are always physically larger than consumers
Energy is lost at each trophic transfer, so less is available higher up
There are always more individuals at lower levels
Biomass increases with each trophic level
questions.explain: Energy decreases at every transfer, so a pyramid of energy is invariably upright, unlike pyramids of numbers or biomass which can be inverted.

questions.q: Pollination by insects is an example of which category of ecosystem service?
questions.explain: Pollination is a supporting and regulating service that underpins food production and ecosystem functioning.

questions.q: In Simpson's index calculation, n usually represents:
options: The total number of individuals of all species
The number of individuals of a particular species
questions.explain: In Simpson's index, n is the number of organisms of a given species and N is the total of all individuals.

questions.q: The competitive exclusion principle states that:
options: Predators and prey cannot share a habitat
Two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely in the same habitat
questions.explain: The competitive exclusion principle holds that two species with identical resource requirements cannot coexist stably; one outcompetes the other.

questions.q: Which of the following is a density-dependent limiting factor on a population?
options: Competition for food as population density rises
questions.explain: Density-dependent factors such as competition, predation and disease intensify as population density increases, while climatic events are density-independent.

questions.q: The final, relatively stable community reached at the end of a successional sequence is called the:
questions.explain: The climax community is the stable, self-sustaining end-point of succession, in equilibrium with prevailing environmental conditions.

questions.q: A pyramid of numbers can appear inverted when:
options: Many small producers support a few large consumers
Decomposers are excluded from the count
Energy increases up the food chain
One large producer such as a tree supports many smaller consumers
questions.explain: A single large producer (e.g. an oak tree) can support many primary consumers (e.g. insects), giving a narrow base and inverted pyramid of numbers.

questions.q: The carrying capacity of an environment is best defined as the:
options: Minimum population needed to avoid extinction
Rate at which a population grows exponentially
Maximum population size that the environment can sustainably support
Total number of trophic levels present
questions.explain: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum population size that the available resources of an environment can support over time.

questions.q: A key advantage of in-situ over ex-situ conservation is that it:
options: Removes the need for protected areas
Maintains species within functioning ecosystems and natural selection
questions.explain: In-situ conservation keeps species in their ecosystem so ecological interactions and natural selection continue.

questions.q: CITES is an international agreement that primarily regulates:
questions.explain: CITES (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) controls cross-border trade in threatened species.

questions.q: The view that species have a right to exist regardless of their usefulness to humans reflects their:
questions.explain: Intrinsic value is the inherent worth of an organism independent of any benefit it provides to people.

questions.q: An S-shaped (sigmoidal) population growth curve differs from a J-shaped curve because the S-curve:
options: Always ends in a population crash
Levels off as the population approaches carrying capacity
questions.explain: An S-curve shows growth slowing and stabilising near carrying capacity as limiting factors increase, unlike unchecked J-curve exponential growth.

questions.q: In the nitrogen cycle, the process of nitrification involves:
options: Conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonium
Conversion of nitrate into nitrogen gas
Uptake of nitrate by plant roots
Conversion of ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate by bacteria
questions.explain: Nitrification is the oxidation of ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate by nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter.

questions.q: The first species to colonise bare rock in primary succession, such as lichens, are known as:
questions.explain: Pioneer species like lichens and mosses are the first colonisers, tolerating harsh conditions and beginning soil formation.

questions.q: An invasive non-native species typically reduces native biodiversity by:
options: Outcompeting or preying on native species
questions.explain: Invasive species often outcompete, predate or introduce disease to natives that lack co-evolved defences.

questions.q: The acronym HIPPO lists major drivers of biodiversity loss. The first 'H' stands for:
questions.explain: In HIPPO, H is Habitat destruction, the single largest cause of biodiversity loss worldwide.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of ex-situ conservation?
questions.explain: Seed banks conserve genetic material away from the natural habitat, making them an ex-situ method.

questions.q: A captive breeding programme that aims to release animals back into the wild is most useful when:
options: The wild habitat has been completely destroyed
Suitable habitat still exists or can be restored
questions.explain: Reintroductions only succeed where suitable habitat remains or can be restored to receive released animals.

questions.q: K-strategist species are generally characterised by:
options: Producing very large numbers of offspring with no parental care
Being the first colonisers of bare rock
Few offspring, large body size, long lifespan and significant parental investment
questions.explain: K-strategists invest heavily in few offspring, are larger and longer-lived, and maintain populations near carrying capacity in stable habitats.

questions.q: In the nitrogen cycle, nitrogen fixation is the conversion of:
options: Atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia or ammonium
questions.explain: Nitrogen fixation converts inert atmospheric N2 into ammonia or ammonium, carried out by bacteria such as Rhizobium and by lightning.

questions.q: Ecological efficiency between two trophic levels is best defined as the:
options: Ratio of energy passed on to a level to the energy received by the level below it
Number of species at a trophic level
questions.explain: Ecological efficiency is the proportion of energy received at one trophic level that is passed on to the next, typically around 10%.

questions.q: Which IUCN category means a species survives only in cultivation or captivity?
questions.explain: Extinct in the Wild means no wild individuals remain and the species persists only in captivity or cultivation.

questions.q: Which term refers to the variety of genes within a single population or species?
questions.explain: Genetic diversity describes the variation of alleles and genes within and between populations of a species.

questions.q: Primary succession differs from secondary succession because primary succession:
options: Always reaches a climax community faster
Begins on newly exposed bare substrate with no pre-existing soil
Cannot result in a climax community
Begins on previously colonised soil after a disturbance
questions.explain: Primary succession starts on lifeless substrate such as bare rock or lava lacking soil, whereas secondary succession begins where soil already exists.

questions.q: In a classic predator-prey relationship, a rise in the prey population is usually followed by:
options: A subsequent rise in the predator population
A permanent fall in prey numbers
An immediate extinction of the predator
questions.explain: More prey provides more food, so the predator population rises after a time lag, which then drives prey numbers back down, producing cyclic oscillations.
